explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Herod, the king, saw that killing James pleased the Jews, and he "proceeded to seize Peter" (Acts 12:3). Peter is one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2). I think this is a heavy turn, because one hard act rolls right into the next.

Not this time, friend. The text says that seeing it pleased the Jews, Herod "proceeded to seize Peter" (Acts 12:3). Peter is one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2). So Herod keeps going instead of stopping, and I think that's a heavy thing to read.

explanations.answer: He sends the church a warning
explanations.explanation: No warning shows up in the text, baker. Herod doesn't send a note or give anyone a heads-up. Seeing that it pleased the Jews, he "proceeded to seize Peter" (Acts 12:3), one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2). The arrest just happens.

Passover is right, friend. Acts 12:4 says Herod "intended to bring him out to the people after the Passover." So the timing is already set in his mind. Peter is sitting in that prison with a clock running.

Close, since the Sabbath was a big day for the people, but it's not what the verse says. Acts 12:4 says Herod "intended to bring him out to the people after the Passover." The arrest happened during the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Acts 12:3), so the Passover is the one on the calendar here.
Good guess for a feast day, baker, but Pentecost isn't named here. Acts 12:4 says Herod "intended to bring him out to the people after the Passover." That's the date Herod has in mind for Peter.

True, baker! Acts 12:5 says that while Peter was kept in prison, "the church was fervently praying to God for him." Peter is locked up, and the church is praying hard. That sentence sits right in the middle of a very tense story.

It's actually true, friend. Acts 12:5 says, "So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was fervently praying to God for him." Notice that word "but." Peter is behind bars, and the church is praying hard on the outside.
Sleeping, yes! Acts 12:6 says Peter was "sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains." The trial is the next day, and he's out cold. Me, I'd be staring at the ceiling counting cookie sheets.

It's a natural guess, baker, since Acts 12:5 says the church was praying. But the text says Peter himself was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains (Acts 12:6). The praying is happening outside the prison, and Peter is the one snoozing.
Nice idea, but no song shows up here, friend. Acts 12:6 says Peter was "sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains." The night before his trial, he's asleep.
True, baker. After the angel says, "Get up quickly," Acts 12:7 says "the chains fell off his wrists." Nobody picks a lock or pulls out a key. The chains just fall off.
It's true, friend. Acts 12:7 says the angel woke Peter, told him, "Get up quickly," and then "the chains fell off his wrists." Two soldiers were right beside him, and the chains came off anyway.

You got it, baker. Acts 12:9 says Peter followed the angel out, "but he was unaware that what the angel was doing was real. He thought he was only seeing a vision." So he's walking out of prison and thinks it's a dream. I'd be pinching myself the whole way.

explanations.answer: The guards are setting a trap
explanations.explanation: Fair guess, friend, but the text doesn't say that. Acts 12:9 says Peter "thought he was only seeing a vision." He doesn't suspect a trap, because he doesn't yet know it's real.

explanations.answer: Herod has decided to free him
explanations.explanation: Not in this story, baker. Acts 12:9 says Peter "was unaware that what the angel was doing was real. He thought he was only seeing a vision." Later he says it was the Lord who "rescued me from Herod’s grasp" (Acts 12:11), so Herod is the one he got away from.

explanations.answer: It opens for them by itself
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Acts 12:10 says the iron gate leading to the city "opened for them by itself." Nobody turns a key or pushes a bar. They walk right through.

explanations.answer: The angel breaks the lock off
explanations.explanation: That's a fun picture, friend, but the text doesn't say it. Acts 12:10 says the iron gate "opened for them by itself." There's no breaking and no force.

explanations.answer: A guard unlocks it for them
explanations.explanation: No guard helps them out, baker. Acts 12:10 says they passed the first and second guards, and then the iron gate "opened for them by itself." Nobody turned a key.

Not quite, friend. Acts 12:10 says that after they walked the length of one block, "the angel suddenly left him." Then Acts 12:11 says Peter "came to himself" on the street. After he realized what had happened, he went to the house on his own (Acts 12:12).

That's right, baker. Acts 12:10 says that after they walked one block, "the angel suddenly left him." Then Peter came to himself in the street (Acts 12:11). Acts 12:12 says that once he realized what had happened, he went to the house.

explanations.answer: The Lord sent His angel to rescue him
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Peter says, "Now I know for sure that the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me from Herod’s grasp…" (Acts 12:11). Before, he thought it was a vision. Now it's clear to him that it's real.

explanations.answer: The guards let him go on purpose
explanations.explanation: No, baker. Peter's own words in Acts 12:11 are, "Now I know for sure that the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me…" The guards never let him go, and the next morning the soldiers are in "no small commotion" about where he went (Acts 12:18).

explanations.answer: Herod changed his mind about him
explanations.explanation: Herod doesn't change his mind, friend. Peter says the Lord "rescued me from Herod’s grasp" (Acts 12:11). Later Herod searches for Peter and can't find him (Acts 12:19). So Peter got away from him.

explanations.answer: Runs inside and leaves the gate shut
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Rhoda, the servant girl at Mary's house, was "so overjoyed that she forgot to open the gate, but ran inside" (Acts 12:14). I've forgotten plenty of things when I got excited, but a whole gate takes talent. Peter was standing out there the whole time.

explanations.answer: Throws the gate wide open for him
explanations.explanation: That would be the sensible move, friend, but it's not what happens. Rhoda was so overjoyed that she "forgot to open the gate, but ran inside and announced, ‘Peter is standing at the gate!’" (Acts 12:14). The gate stays shut, and Peter keeps knocking.

explanations.answer: Faints right there at the gate
explanations.explanation: She's overjoyed, but she doesn't faint, baker. Acts 12:14 says Rhoda "forgot to open the gate, but ran inside" to announce that Peter was there. She's got plenty of energy, just not a lot of gate-opening.
Not so fast, friend. They tell Rhoda, "You are out of your mind" (Acts 12:15). Even when she kept insisting, they said, "It must be his angel." So no, they don't believe her right away.

That's right, baker. Acts 12:15 says they told her, "You are out of your mind." When she kept insisting, they said, "It must be his angel." These are the same people who had gathered to pray (Acts 12:12), and they still need a minute.
Astounded, baker! Acts 12:16 says Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened the door and saw him, "they were astounded." He was standing right there at the door, just like Rhoda said.
No anger here, friend. Acts 12:16 says that when they opened the door and saw Peter, "they were astounded." They'd been praying, and now he's in front of them.
Nobody's disappointed, baker. Acts 12:16 says that when they finally opened the door and saw Peter, "they were astounded." Peter had kept on knocking, and now he's standing in front of them.
That's it, friend. After telling them to send word to James and the brothers, Peter "left for another place" (Acts 12:17). The text doesn't say where. I'll leave it open, same as the verse does.

explanations.answer: He stays the night at Mary's
explanations.explanation: The text says otherwise, baker. After Peter gave his message, he "left for another place" (Acts 12:17). Nothing is said about him staying the night.

explanations.answer: He goes back to face Herod
explanations.explanation: No, friend. Acts 12:17 says Peter "left for another place." The next morning Herod searches for him and can't find him (Acts 12:19), so Peter isn't back at Herod's door.

That's what the text says, baker. After Herod searched for Peter without finding him, "he examined the guards and ordered that they be executed" (Acts 12:19). I think this one is heavy, so I'll let it sit. It tells us what kind of ruler Herod is.

explanations.answer: That the guards be locked up
explanations.explanation: That would be a lighter outcome, friend, but it's not what the text says. Acts 12:19 says Herod "examined the guards and ordered that they be executed." I think this is a heavy verse, and it shows how serious Herod was.

explanations.answer: That the guards be sent home
explanations.explanation: No, baker. Acts 12:19 says that after searching for Peter unsuccessfully, Herod "examined the guards and ordered that they be executed." It's a heavy verse, and I think it's one to read slowly.

Food, baker. Acts 12:20 says they asked for peace "because their region depended on the king’s country for food." Tyre and Sidon needed what Herod's country supplied, so they weren't about to stay in a fight.

Reasonable guess, friend, but the verse names something else. Acts 12:20 says the people of Tyre and Sidon asked for peace "because their region depended on the king’s country for food." Water isn't mentioned.
The text doesn't say that, baker. Acts 12:20 says they asked for peace "because their region depended on the king’s country for food." It's about what was on their tables.

explanations.answer: It's the voice of a god
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The people shout, "This is the voice of a god, not a man!" (Acts 12:22). That's a lot of praise to pile on a man in royal robes. And they said it about a man, not about God.

explanations.answer: It's the voice of a prophet
explanations.explanation: A prophet speaks for God, friend, and that's not what they shout. Acts 12:22 says, "This is the voice of a god, not a man!" They called Herod's voice a god's voice.

explanations.answer: It's the voice of a true king
explanations.explanation: Herod already is a king, so this would have been a smaller compliment, baker. The crowd shouts something bigger: "This is the voice of a god, not a man!" (Acts 12:22).

Glory, friend. Acts 12:23 says that "because Herod did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down." The crowd had just called his voice the voice of a god (Acts 12:22). The text gives that reason itself.
Tithes aren't mentioned, baker. Acts 12:23 says it was "because Herod did not give glory to God" that the angel of the Lord struck him down. The verse gives that reason itself.
No sacrifices show up in this verse, friend. Acts 12:23 says, "because Herod did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down." Glory is the word the text uses.

Jerusalem, baker. Acts 12:25 says Barnabas and Saul "had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem" and then returned. Their church in Antioch had sent relief there earlier in the chapter's story (Acts 11:29-30).
Not Damascus, friend. Acts 12:25 says Barnabas and Saul "had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem." Damascus isn't named in this passage.
Tarsus isn't the one, baker. Acts 12:25 says Barnabas and Saul "had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem" before they returned. Tarsus isn't named in this passage.
